papers.title: Matter that learns what matters
papers.abstract: Can a material learn what deserves its attention? We show this in a model optical network, where action outcomes train a persistent record in each link. The record biases whether a source is consulted and sets how strongly it changes a stored answer, so useful sources gain attention and influence without being identified in advance. The network's experience thus shapes the information available for its future learning. Resonant readouts make this learning fragile: reinforcement can carry a record past resonance, where it persists but its influence weakens. We derive bounds within which relevant signals guide the answer, irrelevant signals are rejected and stored answers remain open to revision. These bounds guide a learning rule that limits reinforcement as records form; in simulations, it acquires useful records and keeps them functional. When relevance changes, an obsolete record can block its own replacement. A local state that strengthens negative writing after unsuccessful actions releases obsolete records and completes the learning sequence more often. A reduced stochastic model, calibrated retrospectively from local response statistics, accounts for changes in sequence completion across writing rules without fitting the aggregate success rates. How a memory is read should decide how it is written.

papers.title: Self-consistent analysis of the Kuramoto model with higher-order interactions
papers.abstract: The Kuramoto model with higher-order interactions has recently been shown to exhibit bistability, explosive synchronization transitions, and rich collective dynamics. Existing analytical approaches, however, typically rely on all-to-all coupling or mean-field approximations of the underlying hypergraph structure. While these methods describe typical networks in the thermodynamic limit, they generally fail to capture the effects of finite hypergraph and oscillator frequency realizations. To address this limitation, we develop a self-consistent analytical framework for the Kuramoto model with dyadic and triadic interactions on hypergraphs. We introduce generalized local order parameters that capture the combined effects of dyadic and triadic phase correlations, and derive a hierarchy of approximation schemes for the local and global synchronization order parameters. Using these approximations, we determine critical coupling strengths for the onset of synchronization and bistability. In particular, we show that the critical triadic coupling strength governing the onset of bistability depends on correlations between the eigenvectors of the dyadic adjacency matrix and the triadic interaction structure. Numerical simulations on homogeneous and heterogeneous hypergraphs validate the theory and illustrate the distinct regimes of applicability of the approximation schemes.

papers.title: Optic flow in the visual system determines interaction force and collective motion
papers.abstract: Collective motion in animal groups relies on visual cues, yet how individual sensory inputs translate into group-level dynamics remains unclear. Traditional models often assume pre-defined ``3A" rules - avoidance, attraction, and alignment - which require agents to directly access the exact positions and velocities of their neighbors. Here, we propose a minimal model based on fundamental visual processing shared across species: detection of image size and optic flow. We show that the collective patterns, such as vortex and polarized school, emerge spontaneously from the competition between image-size-driven avoidance and optic-flow-driven approach. We find that alignment does not require a pre-assumed velocity-matching rule; instead, it arises from the acceleration of an agent toward regions of strong optic flow. The model shows scale-free velocity correlations and topological visual features observed in animal groups. Our results indicate that the phenomenological 3A forces are not irreducible physical rules, but rather emergent outcomes of basic sensorimotor feedback. This framework provides a physical perspective for linking sensory inputs to macroscopic collective behaviors.

papers.title: Emergence and coexistence of periodic and unstructured motion in future-avoiding random walks
papers.abstract: Self-avoiding random walks on graphs can be seen as walkers interacting with their own past history. Here, we consider a complementary class of dynamics, mutual future-avoiding random walks (MFARWs), where stochastically driven walkers are avoiding each other's planned future trajectories. Such systems arise naturally in conceptual models of shared mobility. We show that periodic behavior emerges spontaneously in two different MFARWs, and that periodic and unstructured behavior coexist, providing an example of chimera like behavior of nonoscillatory paths on networks. Further, we analytically describe and predict the onset of structure. We find that the transition from unstructured to periodic behavior is driven by a mechanism of self-amplifying coupling to the periodic components of the stochastic drivers of the system. In the context of shared mobility applications, these states imply a regime of naturally stable coexistence between flexible and line-based public transport.
